system-design-1.pitch: A URL shortener maps a long URL to a short key and redirects on lookup.
system-design-1.definition: Design a service that turns a long URL into a short code and redirects users back. The core is generating a unique short key (base62 of an auto-increment id or a hash), storing the key -> URL mapping in a fast key-value store, and on a GET to the short link returning a 301/302 redirect. It is read-heavy, so you cache hot keys and scale reads horizontally.

diagram.title: URL shortener
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> S[Shorten/Redirect Service]
  S --> C[(Cache)]
  S --> DB[(KV Store)]

keyPoints: Short key: base62 of an id or hash
KV store maps key -> long URL

system-design-2.pitch: A distributed cache shards an in-memory KV store across nodes with replicas.
system-design-2.definition: Design an in-memory key-value cache like Redis serving low-latency reads/writes at scale. Keys are partitioned across nodes by consistent hashing, each shard has replicas for availability, and an eviction policy (LRU/LFU) plus TTLs bound memory. Clients route to the right node, and you choose a consistency/replication model based on whether you favor availability or strong consistency.

diagram.title: Distributed cache
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> R[Router]
  R --> N1[Shard 1 + Replica]
  R --> N2[Shard 2 + Replica]
  R --> N3[Shard 3 + Replica]

keyPoints: Consistent hashing shards keys across nodes

system-design-3.pitch: A chat app uses persistent connections, a message queue and fan-out.
system-design-3.definition: Design a real-time messaging app like WhatsApp. Clients hold a persistent connection (WebSocket) to gateway servers; messages go through a queue to a delivery service that writes to a per-conversation store and pushes to recipients online, or stores for offline delivery. You track delivery/read receipts, fan out to group members, and shard storage by conversation for scale.

diagram.title: Chat application
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Client A] --> G[WebSocket Gateway]
  G --> Q[Message Queue]
  Q --> D[Delivery Service]
  D --> DB[(Message Store)]
  D --> B[Client B]

system-design-4.pitch: A notification system fans events out to subscribers via pub/sub.
system-design-4.definition: Design a system that pushes real-time notifications to users. Producers publish events to a pub/sub broker; a fan-out service resolves subscribers and delivers via WebSocket/push for online users or queues for offline. You decouple producers from delivery, support multiple channels, and scale the broker by topic partitioning.

diagram.title: Real-time notifications
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P[Producer] --> B[Pub/Sub Broker]
  B --> F[Fan-out Service]
  F --> WS[WebSocket Push]
  F --> Q[Offline Queue]

keyPoints: Producers publish events to a broker
WebSocket/push for online, queue for offline

system-design-5.pitch: A file storage service splits files into chunks over blob storage + metadata.
system-design-5.definition: Design a Drive/Dropbox-like service. Files are split into chunks, deduplicated by content hash, and stored in object/blob storage, while a metadata DB tracks files, versions, permissions and chunk maps. Clients sync via a delta/diff protocol, and a CDN speeds downloads. Chunking enables dedup, resumable uploads and efficient sync.

diagram.title: File storage service
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Client] --> API[API]
  API --> M[(Metadata DB)]
  API --> B[(Blob Storage)]
  B --> CDN[CDN] --> U

keyPoints: Chunk files; dedup by content hash
Metadata DB: files, versions, ACLs, chunk map

system-design-6.pitch: Video streaming transcodes to adaptive bitrates and serves via CDN.
system-design-6.definition: Design a YouTube/Netflix-style platform. Uploaded videos are transcoded into multiple resolutions/bitrates and segmented (HLS/DASH), stored in blob storage, and served from a CDN close to users with adaptive bitrate streaming. Metadata and a recommendation/search layer sit in front, and the read path is CDN-heavy for scale.

diagram.title: Video streaming
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Uploader] --> T[Transcoder]
  T --> B[(Blob Storage)]
  B --> CDN[CDN]
  V[Viewer] --> CDN

keyPoints: Segment videos; store in blob storage

system-design-7.pitch: Food delivery matches orders to restaurants and nearby delivery agents.
system-design-7.definition: Design a Swiggy/Zomato-style system. Core services handle restaurant catalog, cart/order, payment, and a matching/dispatch service that assigns nearby delivery partners using their live location (geospatial index). Real-time tracking streams agent location to the customer, and an event-driven design keeps order state in sync across services.

diagram.title: Food delivery
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Customer] --> O[Order Service]
  O --> P[Payment]
  O --> M[Matching/Dispatch]
  M --> A[Delivery Agent]
  A --> L[Location Stream] --> C

keyPoints: Geospatial index to find nearby agents

system-design-8.pitch: Ride-sharing matches riders to drivers using live geospatial data.
system-design-8.definition: Design an Uber-style app. Drivers stream GPS location into a geospatial index (e.g. quadtree/geohash); when a rider requests, a matching service finds nearby drivers, applies surge pricing, and dispatches. Trip and location updates flow over real-time channels, and payments/ratings happen at trip end. The hard parts are low-latency matching and high-frequency location updates.

diagram.title: Ride sharing
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  D[Drivers] --> G[Geo Index]
  R[Rider] --> M[Matching Service]
  M --> G
  M --> T[Trip Service]
  T --> P[Payment]

keyPoints: Drivers stream location to a geo index
Payment and rating at trip end

system-design-9.pitch: E-commerce composes catalog, cart, order, inventory, payment and search.
system-design-9.definition: Design an Amazon-style platform as microservices: a product catalog with search, cart, order and payment services, an inventory service guarding stock, and async fulfillment. Reads (catalog/search) are cache- and CDN-heavy; writes (orders/inventory) need consistency and idempotency. Events coordinate order -> payment -> inventory -> shipping.

diagram.title: E-commerce platform
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> G[API Gateway]
  G --> Cat[Catalog/Search]
  G --> Cart[Cart]
  G --> Ord[Order]
  Ord --> Pay[Payment]
  Ord --> Inv[Inventory]

system-design-10.pitch: A payment gateway tokenizes cards and processes charges idempotently.
system-design-10.definition: Design a payment gateway that securely processes transactions. It tokenizes card data (PCI-DSS scope minimized), forwards charges to acquiring banks/processors, records every state change in an immutable ledger, and uses idempotency keys so retries never double-charge. Webhooks and reconciliation handle async results and failures.

diagram.title: Payment gateway
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  M[Merchant] --> G[Gateway]
  G --> V[Tokenize/Validate]
  V --> P[Processor/Bank]
  G --> L[(Ledger)]
  P --> W[Webhook] --> M

system-design-11.pitch: Hotel booking guards room inventory with availability and locking.
system-design-11.definition: Design a hotel booking system. Core pieces are a search/availability service over room inventory by date range, a booking service that reserves rooms with a short-lived lock to prevent double-booking, payment, and confirmation. Availability is read-heavy (cached); booking needs transactional consistency on the inventory.

diagram.title: Hotel booking
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> S[Search/Availability]
  S --> Inv[(Inventory)]
  U --> B[Booking Service]
  B --> Inv
  B --> P[Payment]

keyPoints: Reserve with a short lock to avoid double-book

system-design-12.pitch: Ticket booking handles seat selection with concurrency-safe locking.
system-design-12.definition: Design a movie/flight/train ticket system. The crux is concurrency: many users compete for the same seats, so you hold a temporary seat lock/reservation (with timeout) during checkout, confirm on payment, and release on timeout. Inventory updates are transactional, and read paths (showtimes/seat maps) are cached.

diagram.title: Ticket booking
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> Seat[Seat Service]
  Seat --> Lock[(Lock/Reservation)]
  U --> Pay[Payment]
  Pay --> Confirm[Confirm Booking]
  Confirm --> DB[(Bookings)]

keyPoints: Confirm on payment; release on timeout

system-design-13.pitch: A social platform combines a social graph, feed and media at scale.
system-design-13.definition: Design a Facebook/Instagram-style platform. Key parts are a social graph (followers/friends), a post/media service backed by blob storage + CDN, and a news feed built by fan-out. Reads dominate, so you cache aggressively and pre-compute feeds; writes propagate via events. Celebrity accounts force a hybrid fan-out strategy.

diagram.title: Social media platform
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> G[API Gateway]
  G --> Graph[Social Graph]
  G --> Post[Post/Media]
  Post --> CDN[CDN]
  G --> Feed[Feed Service] --> Cache[(Feed Cache)]

keyPoints: Posts + media in blob storage + CDN

system-design-14.pitch: A news feed pre-computes or assembles ranked posts per user.
system-design-14.definition: Design a news feed. The central decision is fan-out on write (push each post into followers' feeds, fast reads, costly for big accounts) versus fan-out on read (assemble the feed at request time, cheap writes, slower reads). Most systems use a hybrid, rank posts by a relevance model, and cache assembled feeds.
keyPoints: Fan-out on write vs read (or hybrid)

system-design-15.pitch: A rate limiter caps request rate using counters in a shared store.
system-design-15.definition: Design an API rate limiter that throttles clients to N requests per window. Common algorithms are token bucket (smooth bursts) and sliding window (accurate). Counters live in a fast shared store (Redis) keyed by client/API so limits hold across distributed instances, returning 429 when exceeded.

diagram.title: Rate limiter
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> RL[Rate Limiter]
  RL --> R[(Redis Counters)]
  RL -->|under limit| API[API]
  RL -->|over limit| X[429]

keyPoints: Token bucket or sliding window algorithm
Counters in Redis keyed by client/API

system-design-16.pitch: Logging/monitoring ingests, stores and alerts on telemetry at scale.
system-design-16.definition: Design a logging and monitoring platform. Agents ship logs/metrics to an ingestion pipeline (often a queue), which indexes them into a searchable, time-series store; dashboards query it and an alerting engine evaluates rules to page on-call. The pipeline must absorb spikes (buffering) and retain data cost-effectively (tiered storage).

diagram.title: Logging & monitoring
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Agents] --> Q[Ingestion Queue]
  Q --> I[Index/Store]
  I --> D[Dashboards]
  I --> AL[Alerting] --> O[On-call]

system-design-17.pitch: A distributed scheduler runs jobs reliably with leader election and retries.
system-design-17.definition: Design a system that schedules and runs jobs at the right time across a cluster. A durable store holds job definitions and next-run times; scheduler nodes use leader election (or partitioning) to avoid double-execution, push due jobs onto a queue, and workers execute with retries and idempotency. Missed runs and failures are tracked.

diagram.title: Distributed job scheduler
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  DB[(Job Store)] --> S[Scheduler Leader]
  S --> Q[Job Queue]
  Q --> W1[Worker]
  Q --> W2[Worker]

keyPoints: Durable job store with next-run times

system-design-18.pitch: Autocomplete serves ranked prefix matches from a trie/index fast.
system-design-18.definition: Design a search autocomplete. Queries are matched by prefix using a trie or an inverted/prefix index, ranked by popularity/recency, and served from memory with heavy caching for single-digit-millisecond responses. Suggestions are precomputed and updated from query logs offline.

diagram.title: Search autocomplete
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User keystrokes] --> S[Suggest Service]
  S --> T[Trie/Prefix Index]
  S --> C[(Cache)]
  Logs[Query Logs] --> B[Offline Builder] --> T

system-design-19.pitch: A recommender combines offline models with online serving.
system-design-19.definition: Design a recommendation engine. It blends collaborative filtering (users like you) and content-based filtering (similar items), trained offline on interaction data into a model/embeddings, then serves real-time candidate generation + ranking at request time. Feedback loops continuously improve the model, and results are cached per user.

diagram.title: Recommendation engine
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  E[Events] --> Train[Offline Training]
  Train --> M[Model/Embeddings]
  U[User] --> Serve[Ranking Service]
  Serve --> M
  Serve --> C[(Cache)]

system-design-20.pitch: Order management splits into services coordinated by a saga.
system-design-20.definition: Design a microservices order system. Order, payment, inventory and shipping are separate services; an order is a distributed transaction coordinated by a saga (orchestrated or choreographed) with compensating actions on failure. Services communicate via events for loose coupling, behind an API gateway, each owning its data.

diagram.title: Order management (microservices)
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  G[API Gateway] --> O[Order]
  O --> P[Payment]
  O --> I[Inventory]
  O --> S[Shipping]
  O --> E[(Event Bus)]

keyPoints: Event-driven, each service owns its data

system-design-21.pitch: Auth issues tokens (JWT/OAuth2) and validates them on each request.
system-design-21.definition: Design an authentication and authorization system. An auth/identity service authenticates users and issues short-lived access tokens (JWT) plus refresh tokens via OAuth2 flows; resource services validate the token signature and claims statelessly and enforce RBAC/policies. Refresh tokens are revocable and stored server-side.

diagram.title: Auth system
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> Auth[Auth Service]
  Auth -->|JWT + Refresh| U
  U -->|Bearer JWT| API[Resource Service]
  API -->|Validate + RBAC| API

keyPoints: Identity service issues JWT access tokens

system-design-22.pitch: An API gateway is the single entry that routes, secures and aggregates.
system-design-22.definition: Design an API gateway - the single entry point in front of microservices. It routes requests to the right service, and centralizes cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request/response transformation, caching and aggregation of multiple service calls. It decouples clients from internal service topology.

diagram.title: API gateway
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> GW[API Gateway]
  GW --> S1[Service A]
  GW --> S2[Service B]
  GW --> S3[Service C]

system-design-23.pitch: Real-time inventory keeps stock consistent under concurrent updates.
system-design-23.definition: Design a real-time inventory system. Stock levels change from many sources (orders, returns, restocks), so it is event-driven: each change is an event applied to an authoritative, transactional store, with reservations to prevent overselling and a read model/cache for fast availability checks. Consistency on decrements is the hard part.

diagram.title: Real-time inventory
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Src[Orders/Returns/Restock] --> E[(Event Stream)]
  E --> Inv[Inventory Service]
  Inv --> DB[(Stock Store)]
  Inv --> Cache[(Availability Cache)]

system-design-24.pitch: High availability removes single points of failure with redundancy.
system-design-24.definition: Design a highly available web app that survives failures. Every tier is redundant: stateless app servers behind load balancers across multiple availability zones, replicated databases with failover, health checks that route around dead instances, and no single point of failure. You add auto-scaling, retries with backoff, and graceful degradation.

diagram.title: High availability
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Users] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> A1[App AZ-1]
  LB --> A2[App AZ-2]
  A1 --> DBp[(DB Primary)]
  A2 --> DBr[(DB Replica)]
  DBp -.failover.- DBr

system-design-25.pitch: Multi-tenant SaaS isolates tenants while sharing infrastructure.
system-design-25.definition: Design a multi-tenant SaaS app where many customers share one system safely. The key choice is the isolation model: separate database per tenant (strong isolation, costlier), shared database with separate schemas, or a shared schema with a tenant_id (cheapest, most scalable). Every request carries tenant context, and you enforce isolation, per-tenant config and noisy-neighbor limits.

system-design-26.pitch: A distributed queue decouples producers and consumers durably.
system-design-26.definition: Design a distributed message queue like Kafka/SQS. Producers append messages to partitioned, replicated logs; consumers read at their own offset in groups for parallelism, with at-least-once delivery and durability. Partitioning gives ordering-per-key and horizontal scale; consumers commit offsets to track progress.

diagram.title: Distributed queue
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P[Producers] --> Br[Broker Partitions]
  Br --> C1[Consumer Group A]
  Br --> C2[Consumer Group B]

keyPoints: Producers append; consumers read by offset

system-design-27.pitch: A notification service abstracts Email, SMS and Push behind one API.
system-design-27.definition: Design a multi-channel notification service. A single API accepts a notification request, which is queued and processed by channel adapters (email, SMS, push), each handling provider integration, templating, rate limits and retries. User preferences decide channels, and the queue absorbs spikes and isolates failures per channel.

diagram.title: Notification service
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  App[App] --> API[Notification API]
  API --> Q[Queue]
  Q --> E[Email Adapter]
  Q --> S[SMS Adapter]
  Q --> Pu[Push Adapter]

system-design-28.pitch: A banking system uses ACID, a double-entry ledger and idempotency.
system-design-28.definition: Design a banking transaction system where correctness is paramount. Money movements are recorded in an append-only, double-entry ledger inside ACID transactions so debits and credits always balance; idempotency keys prevent double-processing, and strong consistency beats availability for the core ledger. Async events drive notifications and reporting.

diagram.title: Banking transactions
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> T[Transaction Service]
  T --> L[(Double-entry Ledger)]
  T --> Acc[(Accounts DB)]
  T --> E[(Event Stream)]

system-design-29.pitch: Distributed sessions move state to a shared store, not sticky servers.
system-design-29.definition: Design session management across many app servers. Instead of relying on sticky sessions, you store session state in a fast shared store (Redis) keyed by a session id in a cookie/token, so any server can serve any request - enabling scale and failover. Alternatively, stateless JWTs carry session data client-side with revocation handled separately.
keyPoints: Central session store (Redis) by session id

system-design-30.pitch: An audit trail is an append-only, correlated, tamper-evident log.
system-design-30.definition: Design an audit and logging trail for microservices. Every service emits structured audit events with a correlation id, actor, action and timestamp to a durable append-only store; the trail is immutable and tamper-evident (hash-chained), queryable for compliance, and retained per policy. Correlation ids stitch one user action across services.

diagram.title: Audit trail
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S1[Service A] --> Q[Audit Pipeline]
  S2[Service B] --> Q
  Q --> Store[(Append-only Store)]
  Store --> Query[Compliance Query]

keyPoints: Structured events: actor, action, time, correlation id
